Tips for Enjoying Life with a Chronic Illness Flare-Up 🧠 Dealing with a flare-up can make it hard to keep doing the things you enjoy, but it’s still important to find ways to have fun and stay active. Here are some useful tips that have helped me: Keep it short : If a full evening feels like too much, try going for just an hour or two 🕰️  Plan ahead : Research the nearest toilets at your destination to feel more at ease 💻  Bring a bag : Pack spare clothes, toilet paper, wipes, medications, and anything else you might need 💊  Choose your company : Go with people who understand your condition or do things on your own if it’s more comfortable. Take breaks : Don’t push yourself. Sit down and rest whenever you need to 🫂 Go at quieter times : Visit places when they’re less busy to avoid stress or long waits. Stay local : Stick to nearby spots so you can leave quickly if you need to in an emergency. Be flexible : It’s okay to change or cancel plans if you’re not feeling well. Always make sure that you’re prioritising your health💜 These small adjustments help make it easier to still do the things I enjoy, even during flare-ups🤝🏼 . . . #ulcerativecolitis #colitis #flareup #chronicillness #fatigue #colitisfighter #colitisawareness #mentalhealth #mentalhealthawareness #mentalhealthmatters #usefultips #useful

Endo and colitis are flaring up again , causing me pain and serious fatigue, and also blood loss. The fatigue is absolutely draining. i thought it was due to being starving, where u feel u need a good meal to get energised,  but it's my body going into a flare.  Thank goodness I have a hospital appointment today.  Bloating causes me so much water retention, and it shows in this reel. Abs still holding on strong,  my lower stomach section is hard and sore, but I'm not giving up easily,  not a chance. I was going to cover up in the gym this morning, but why should I? This is me, and it's not my fault  Chronic illnesses are no joke. They just appear whenever they want and when you least expect it. Last year I was in hospital days after my birthday with colitis & almost went into septic shock ☠️ even the morphine I couldn’t enjoy 🙈 This year I’m up at 4am to meditate and go for a run at 6am!!  Funny what can change when you change.  This birthday was my best yet, was it fancy?  Did I travel?  Go for luxury dinner?  Spend time with lots of people?  Get drunk?  No.  To all of the above.  I focused on myself.  I changed my routine.  I meditated, went for a run, a swim & sauna and brunch!  I didn’t drink a drop of alcohol.  Altho … 🍄 I did 🙊🦄🤣  I watched my favourite movie and ate pizza and went to bed at 8pm 🤣 It was the best bday ever, I feel in the best head & heart space. Why?  I’m doing life my way.  I’m not doing it for other people and what is expected on your bday.  I care deeply about my mental, physical & emotional health because I have suffered with all of them.  So I choose to do things that elevate me and this is what it is for me. It’s different for everyone.  I’m not showing this to say you should do the same.  I’m showing this to say “do what you wanna do with your life”  However “different” it is to everyone else.  Choose to be yourself. Choose to make yourself happy. Choose to live life on your terms.  Step one: figure out wtf that is baby.  How do you feel about birthdays? It’s always a touchy subject, it doesn’t need to be. Celebrate yourself! You’re going to die one day, enjoy it while it lasts 🫶🏼 Lots of love,  Rebecca xxx #birthdaygirl #birthdaylove #doingthingsdifferently #mywayorthehighway #5amclub #4amclub #morningperson #morningroutine #howyoustartyourday #runnersofinsta #couchto5k #routine #consistency #colitis #chronicillness #mentalhealthmatters #fyppppppppppppppppppppppp

These 2 pictures show my son at the start of year 9 and the end of year 9. If you would’ve told me that in the course of a year his health would decline so quickly, i could never imagine just how much.  In the first picture, he was over 9 stone, eating anything and everything and living a normal life. We knew he had stomach issues and food intolerances but it wasn’t too bad.  Fast forward to the second picture nearly a year later and he was very unwell. He weighed 6 stone 9 and couldn’t tolerate food and drink without being sick and going to the toilet. This goes to show how quickly IBD can take a hold and be a dangerous disease if left untreated. It scared my husband and I because he was shaking uncontrollably and we didnt know why the medications weren’t helping at all.  I called the hospital who said to bring him in and they would find a bed. They were amazing and put him in a side room in A&E with a bathroom until they had a bed.  He saw a professor who was brilliant. He looked at his previous MRI, blood results and felt his stomach. He said he was close to blockage due to one of the strictures and would have to go onto liquid diet via NG for a while. Here is the paradox: a diagnosis of an incurable chronic condition can be very overwhelming and discouraging. However, it can also push you in the right direction. I'm not trying to be overly positive about this, but you can fight back and still live life to the fullest despite health hurdles. It took me a good few years to start recognizing that I should be proud of what I have achieved despite my health obstacles. Even though I am currently experiencing a spell of good health, my IBD will probably flare up again at some point. That's okay, I feel prepared and ready. I don't see my Ulcerative Colitis as my enemy, nor am I trying to befriend it. I view it as a factor that influences how I need to shape my lifestyle to make the most of what I have. Even though I'm not always successful in getting my message across, I continue to try to show fellow IBD-ers that it is possible to live your life with IBD as an extra, rather than the main character. Things ticked along over the next few months. He continued on feeds and went into year 10 with the NG tube and steroid bloat. We were so worried how he wouid get on as school can be a hard place to look so different but his school and friends were amazing, it was a huge relief.  He needed another iron infusion and continued with infliximab alongside tapering the steroids. We saw a change in his symptoms so were really positive. He was having weekly blood tests and we never had any concerns as didn’t heard back from them.  Then one day, after he had been to the toilet and flushed, I saw the toilet pan was full of blood. Instant panic came over me and I asked my son if he had seen it. He said he hadn’t but I’m not sure if he just felt it was easier to ignore it as he was on treatment.  Our sons care is shared between 2 hospitals and unfortunately the local hospital who was completing the infusions and bloods doesn’t have the best track record. I rang his consultant to say he was bleeding again. She called me back and said they had missed his blood and stool results showing his levels were through the roof and they needed to give him a double dose of infliximab urgently. As you can imagine we weren’t happy that this had been missed. The consultant was very apologetic and honest explaining they had missed this and it wasn’t acceptable.  So he went in for his double dose of infliximab to see if that would help. He was also weaning off feeds and was allowed small, bland snacks. He was thrilled at this and enjoyed his first yorkshire pudding in weeks.  #infliximab #iron #ironinfusion #infusion #foodlover #foodtok #nhs #nhsuk #bowel #treatment #feedingtubeawareness #modulen #ngfeedingtube #chronicillnessawareness #chronicillness #teenage #coloplast #crohnscolitisuk #ibdsuperheroes #crohnscolitis #ileostomy #colitis #stomabag #stoma #stomach #fyp #f #disabled #disabledtiktok

Our son has been using the @Coloplast_UK Heylo system for a few weeks now. It is designed to alarm when a leak is starting to happen to help prevent a problem.  He was having quite a few leaks in the night which were not only affecting his sleep, but were also taking a toll mentally. Dealing with everything he has been through all while navigating teenage life must be so hard and then having to deal with a bedtime accident hasn’t been easy. The Heylo has been amazing and has alerted him to any leaks that have started. It first sends a txt like message to his phone which alerts him to check the app. He then checks the app and this tells him which section of the stoma bag it is coming from. He can then look and decide if he needs to add a flange to hold him until he can change or if he needs to change straight away.  He chooses to keep the alarm on silent during the day at college but checks his phone for messages regularly throughout the day, this is because he hasn’t told anyone about his stoma and doesn’t want to explain what the alarm is for yet. He then sets the alarm to go off through the night to wake him if needed.  This system has given him such relief to know that he has the chance to prevent a leak and that is huge for him. It is so easy to use and all the information is on an easy to use app. This really has been a game changer for him and he highly recommends it to anyone considering using it. #nhs #nhsuk #bowel #treatment #feedingtubeawareness #modulen #ngfeedingtube #chronicillnessawareness #chronicillness #teenage #coloplast #crohnscolitisuk #ibdsuperheroes #crohnscolitis #ileostomy #colitis #stoma #ibd #crohnsawareness #crohnsdisease #heylo #fyp #for #stomakid #hospital #disabled #disabledtiktok

These 2 pictures show my son at the start of year 9 and the end of year 9. If you would’ve told me that in the course of a year his health would decline so quickly, i could never imagine just how much.  In the first picture, he was over 9 stone, eating anything and everything and living a normal life. We knew he had stomach issues and food intolerances but it wasn’t too bad.  Fast forward to the second picture nearly a year later and he was very unwell. He weighed 6 stone 9 and couldn’t tolerate food and drink without being sick and going to the toilet. This goes to show how quickly IBD can take a hold and be a dangerous disease if left untreated. We were lucky that he got help straight away but sadly that’s not the case for everyone.  #nhs #bowel #treatment #feedingtubeawareness #modulen #ngfeedingtube #chronicillnessawareness #chronicillness #teenage #coloplast #crohnscolitisuk #ibdsuperheroes #crohnscolitis #ileostomy #colitis #stoma #ibd #ibd #crohnsawareness #crohnsdisease #bowelresection #stomabag #year10 #gcse #father #hospital

So, what’s the deal with Crohn’s, Colitis, and cranberries? Let’s break it down! Studies (mostly on mice) hint that whole cranberries might benefit gut health and even help reduce IBD symptoms. Packed with polyphenols—natural antioxidants—cranberries can help reduce inflammation and support a balanced gut. These polyphenols can feed good bacteria, encouraging a healthier gut environment. Whole cranberries or smoothies are best for fiber, but juice can still give a boost! Polyphenols are also in dark red, purple, and blue fruits and veggies, so keep your plate colorful for a gut-friendly variety. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! Something a little different from me today. I don't usually work weekends but I couldn't turn this one down. I received a message yesterday from a desperate Mum who lives locally to me. She had arranged for a cleaner to come and give her sons room a deep clean. I'm sure they had their reasons but unfortunately they didn't turn up at the last minute. Her son Joe, is 16 and has been battling ulcerative colitis for the past 18 months. The illness has turned his world upside down. He’s missed 8 months of school and was made to sit his GCSEs despite this. It’s also kept him from playing football, the thing he loves to do most. Just two weeks ago, Joe underwent life changing surgery that resulted in a stoma. During this time, the family have been staying at the hospital and understandably, the home has been a little neglected. Tomorrow, he’s finally coming home, and I’m so glad to help create a clean, welcoming space that will hopefully bring him comfort as he begins his recovery and navigates this new chapter of his life. I didn't film too much of the bathroom process but we've also completed this room and I'll be returning later this week to get the rest of the house sorted. It’s National Stress Awareness Day   We know that people with Crohn’s or Colitis are at greater risk of mental health problems like stress, anxiety, and depression than the general population. At the same time, mental health problems, like stress, can have a negative effect on gut symptoms.  People who have both mental health problems and Crohn’s or Colitis can end up in a cycle, with each one making the other worse.   Read more on how reducing stress helped Mike manage his Ulcerative Colitis by going to our link in bio, under “latest news and blogs” and click “Mike’s Story”    Image description: The text reads on an orange and purple background: “The feeling of being in control of my work made a huge difference to me mentally and for my Colitis. Within 6 weeks of leaving that job, I was off steroids and I haven’t experienced a flare-up in over 20 years. - Mike. This summer marked 13 years since I was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease. Back then, I was at my lowest weight of around 40kg. It’s strange, even then I’d get comments like “I wish I was as skinny as you” but also “don’t you eat anything?” Really, all I wanted was a working body. I think it’s easy for people to assume that ‘slimness’ equates to health. But that isn’t strictly true. In my case, and many others with inflammatory bowel disease, it’s not.  We’re thin because our body isn’t absorbing any nutrients from our food, we can’t hold it down, and a multitude of other reasons. In fact, I completely struggled with the thought of being “skinny”. When I was younger I would force myself to drink loads of protein shakes, fast food and one day me and my friend brought 2L tubs of ice cream each and tried to eat them in one sitting. All just so I could try and put on some weight. I would feel panic if I hadn’t eaten for 2 hours. Really, looking back, it’s not a surprise I have crohns 😅 Now, with a lot of healing done and my diet drastically different, majority of it being from fruit and plant foods, my body is able to absorb more and my weight has steadied out to what is considered healthy for me. While I know how we look may not be the most important thing, I know how much having IBD can affect your self confidence, and that’s another reason why I’m on a mission to help as many people as I can!  #crohnsdisease #crohnsawareness #crohnsandcolitis #crohnswarrior #crohnsandcolitisuk #crohnsandcolitisawareness #colitis #ulcerativecolitis #bodyimage #bodyimageissues #bodyimagehealing #healthcoach #healthcoaching #glowyourhealth #healthyeating #healthcoachtips

Endometriosis and its potential link to Crohn’s & Colitis:  Let’s explore! Studies suggest a possible connection between endometriosis and IBD. Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, sometimes affecting the intestines. This can cause chronic inflammation, a key factor in IBD. Research indicates individuals with endometriosis may be at higher risk for IBD, but more research is needed to confirm the exact nature of this relationship. It’s unclear if endometrial tissue directly contributes to IBD or if shared risk factors are involved. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! A few days after the MRI, I received a call from my sons IBD consultant. The minute I saw his missed call so soon after the MRI, I knew something was wrong.  I called him back and he said the MRI had shown only slight improvement in the inflammation but also that one of the strictures hadn’t reacted to the infliximab as well as they had hoped. He explained that it was so narrow it had a back flow of blood and stool trying to push it’s way through. He was very concerned and had already spoken to the surgical team to get some advice.  He said he would need a bowel resection quite quickly and also told us to prepare for a stoma due to the condition his bowel was still in. This all came as a massive shock because we were told that surgery is usually a very last resort, especailly in children.  He asked that we come in the following week for cameras again to take a closer look and to talk through the plan face to face. My son was not happy at having to go through bowel prep again. He was more bothered by that at the time than anything else. I think it turned out to be a good distraction.  #infliximab #iron #ironinfusion #infusion #nhsuk #nhs #bowel #treatment #feedingtubeawareness #modulen #ngfeedingtube #chronicillnessawareness #chronicillness #teenage #coloplast #crohnscolitisuk #ibdsuperheroes #crohnscolitis #fyp #f #bowelresection #hospital #surgery #crohnsdisease #colitis #viral_video #viralvideos

Did you know this was happening around you when you have a CT scan?! CT scans help in IBD to: Diagnose complications like abscesses, fistulas, or strictures. Assess inflammation during a flare. Monitor treatment response. CT technology has improved significantly, especially with speed. Faster scans reduce motion blur, ensuring clearer and more accurate images of the intestines, which are constantly moving. Think of it like a camera with a faster shutter speed—it captures better details in less time. While the scan may seem intimidating, it’s quicker and less uncomfortable than an MRI. See my previous video on sourdoughs benefits in those with IBD. 3️⃣ Pineapple– Contains bromelain, which helps digest proteins. 4️⃣ Kiwi & Papaya– Both are full of digestive enzymes that support healthy digestion. And for a soothing morning drink, I love peppermint tea with honey, of course! Honey contains enzymes that help break down starches and reduces bloating. One more tip is to also control the speed in which you eat! The faster you eat, the more air you’ll be ingesting which will also contribute to bloating! What foods do you find helpful with bloating? What’s the link between Crohn’s, Colitis, and gluten?  Let’s dive in! Research shows celiac disease and IBD are linked—each can raise the risk of the other. Symptoms overlap, with celiac patients often opting for gluten-free diets. But for many with IBD, certain foods, like high-FODMAP bread, can cause bloating and discomfort. Sourdough bread may be gentler on the gut! Its fermentation process reduces gluten and FODMAPs, which can lead to less gas and bloating for those sensitive. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! Did you know Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) can impact your menstrual cycle?  Heavy periods (menorrhagia) are common among those with IBD, and it’s not just about hormones.  Chronic inflammation, anemia from blood loss, and even certain IBD medications can all contribute to heavier or irregular periods.  If you’re experiencing this, it’s important to talk to your doctor—managing IBD and your menstrual health together can make a big difference! Let me know your thoughts in the comments! So, what’s the deal with Crohn’s, Colitis, and cranberries? Let’s break it down! Studies (mostly on mice) hint that whole cranberries might benefit gut health and even help reduce IBD symptoms. Packed with polyphenols—natural antioxidants—cranberries can help reduce inflammation and support a balanced gut. These polyphenols can feed good bacteria, encouraging a healthier gut environment. Whole cranberries or smoothies are best for fiber, but juice can still give a boost! Polyphenols are also in dark red, purple, and blue fruits and veggies, so keep your plate colorful for a gut-friendly variety. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! How does iron deficiency connect to Crohn’s & Colitis? Let’s break it down! Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is common in IBD due to poor iron absorption and blood loss, especially affecting women with heavy periods. Unfortunately, diet alone isn’t enough to fix it. To meet iron needs, you’d need around 100-200 mg of elemental iron daily—more than food alone can provide. While iron-rich foods help, most with IBD need iron supplements or infusions to restore levels. IDA is linked to higher risks of disease progression and hospitalization, making proper management essential. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! If you have IBD, you’re not alone in feeling like you’re wiping a lot after using the bathroom! Here are some strategies to help: Consider a bidet – It’s hygienic and gentle on anal complications like skin tags and fistulas, which wiping can irritate. Watch your diet – Cutting back on fast food, fried foods, and sugary drinks can help clean up your stool and reduce irritation. Bulk up your stool – Include more soluble and insoluble fiber in your meals. Think oats, chia seeds, carrots, apples, and the skins of fruits like pears and grapes. Whole grains like whole wheat and barley are great too. If this issue persists despite dietary changes, consult your gastroenterologist for further evaluation. Women with IBD may experience pelvic discomfort during flares, making it hard to tell whether the pain is from IBD or a gynaecological issue.  Menstrual irregularities and intense abdominal pain can sometimes mimic menstrual cramps. A decidual cast occurs when the uterus sheds its lining in one piece—extremely painful, as the cervix dilates to pass it. While rare, if you pass one, take a pregnancy test, as pregnancy loss can cause similar symptoms. Understanding how IBD and gynaecological symptoms overlap helps ensure you get the right care for both. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! Endometriosis and its potential link to Crohn’s & Colitis:  Let’s explore! Studies suggest a possible connection between endometriosis and IBD. Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, sometimes affecting the intestines. This can cause chronic inflammation, a key factor in IBD. Research indicates individuals with endometriosis may be at higher risk for IBD, but more research is needed to confirm the exact nature of this relationship. It’s unclear if endometrial tissue directly contributes to IBD or if shared risk factors are involved. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! Let me explain… Before I explain, do you think IBD is the same as IBS? Many of you may have heard the terms IBD and IBS being interchanged for one another as if they were the same thing. While it is true that both present with similar symptoms, can be triggered by similar things, they are however not the same. IBD is classified as an actual disease that causes intestinal destruction due to inflammation while IBS is defined as a syndrome, or a disorder of gut function brought about by the control of the gut-brain axis (GBA). Furthermore, the differences don’t stop there as you can see IBD when diagnostic imaging (x-ray, CT, MRI, and ultrasound scans) are used whereas you can’t see IBS on these scans and IBD is associated with an increased risk of developing colon cancer whereas IBS is not. Even though symptoms of IBS (bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and constipation) are like IBD, there are so many other features that separate the two. For example, IBD is associated with fatigue, weight loss, generally feeling unwell, loss of appetite as well as mouth ulcers whereas none of these are present in IBS. The most obvious difference between the two is that the ‘inflammation’ in IBS does not cause destructive damage to the intestines in addition to there is no bleeding after bowel movements in IBS unlike in IBD further differentiating the two. Crohn’s & Colitis awareness week 💜 Part 2 of my IBD story.  I went into a major flare up when I was 22 in 2019 at the time I was on holiday and I had lost an extreme amount of weight, everything I was eating I couldn’t hold down and my stomach pains were excruciating. I couldn’t get of bed and would be curled up in a ball hoping it would pass, it of course did not. Once i got home I was admitted into hospital and my meds changed, I was put onto prednisolone (steroids) aswell as being tube fed. I also had these lumps on my shin that felt bruised but wouldn’t go and this is called Erythema nodosum, this can happen when you have a flare up but I was told it is very rare. I was in for several weeks and sent home on steroids I still wasn’t right and a month later I was back in hospital in even worse pain still on steroids but the dosage was higher. Yet again I was in hospital for several weeks feeling worse than ever. My mental health was at an all time low and I thought these pains were never going to go away. The steroids now at this point kicked in and I was sent home for the final time that year (November 2019).  I then went through the last month and the following year through Covid on steroids at the highest dose and as you can see in pictures Moon face appeared. I was still not at a good weight and I also had started a new infusion Vedolizumab. I had this for a few months but it did not work for me so they carried on giving me steroids. My fatigue was at an all time low, my mood swings on the steroids were terrible and during Covid this wasn’t good (2020) Fast forward to January 2021, I developed a rectovaginal fistula and was admitted to have a seton placed for the fistula. I was sent home but the pain of it was unbearable and things got worse throughout January.   February my health declined and the pain was excruciating i couldn’t sit and would scream in pain. I was admitted and had been told I now had Sepsis and I needed a Stoma bag the following day to give everything a rest and time to heal. I was so scared but knew it was the only way but most importantly this was going to save my life. Crohn’s & Colitis awareness week 💜 A little about my IBD story (it’s a long one so here’s part 1 of the short version 😅) So for those of you who don’t know me I’m Phillipa and I have had Inflammatory Bowel Disease for 19 years. I was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease in 2006 when I was 9 years old. I dropped to 2 stone, I was glued to the toilet 24/7 with constant diarrhoea, my body was also not absorbing any foods I had been eating and I was also in excruciating pains with my stomach and chest I had to be tub fed for a few months which helped me gain weight and brought me out of my first major flare aswell as taking omeprazole a lot for chest pains.  I was always in and out of hospital throughout my childhood and teenage years once I had been diagnosed after the age of 9. Constant blood tests, check ups, hospital stays, colonoscopies, endoscopies, scans, infusions you name it I was in and out ALL OF THE TIME 🫠  and when I turned 14 in 2011 I had another major hospital stay where I was then also diagnosed with Ulcerative Colitis. At this point I was suffering so much with constipation (not going the toilet for over a month at a time) and a lot of bleeding which was extremely painful I then felt scared to go to the toilet. At this time I had been on several immune suppressants and would go in for several colonoscopies and then infusions that being Infliximab.  That kept things at bay for several years after that with the odd little flare and hospital stay here and there and then a medication change to Adulimumab with a combination of Azathioprine when I was 17 for a good 4/5 years and that kept me in remission till I was around 22 years old. My next horrid flare up🫠 If you’ve read up to here thank you for hearing a little of my story (part 1) and il be sharing the next part along with other IBD related things this week! 💜 #ibd #ibdawareness #crohnsdisease #ulcerativecolitis #crohnsandcolitis #inflammatoryboweldisease #chronicillness #crohns #colitis

How does this connect to Crohn’s & Colitis?  Let’s dig in! Eating a fiber-rich diet can reduce inflammation, support immunity, and restore your gut microbiome—key for those with IBD. But remember, gut health isn’t one-size-fits-all! That “slimy” stuff in okra? It’s called mucilage, and it forms a gel that acts like fiber and a prebiotic. It softens stools, making it easier to stay regular—especially helpful for IBD-related constipation! Mucilage is also in chia, flaxseeds, psyllium husk, and aloe vera. It slows digestion, helps you feel full, and feeds good gut bacteria. Okra water is trending, and while it may not beat cooked okra for gut health, it’s safe to try! How do carbs link to Crohn’s & Colitis?  Let’s find out! Cooking and then cooling foods like rice, pasta, and potatoes turns some starch into resistant starch. This starch isn’t digested in the small intestine, so it reaches the colon to feed good gut bacteria. For those with IBD, resistant starch can boost bowel regularity, support a healthier gut, and promote beneficial bacteria like bifidobacteria, which may help reduce inflammation. Plus, resistant starches have a lower glycemic impact, helping with blood sugar and fullness! Let me know your thoughts in the comments! How does iron deficiency connect to Crohn’s & Colitis? Let’s break it down! Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is common in IBD due to poor iron absorption and blood loss, especially affecting women with heavy periods. Unfortunately, diet alone isn’t enough to fix it. To meet iron needs, you’d need around 100-200 mg of elemental iron daily—more than food alone can provide. While iron-rich foods help, most with IBD need iron supplements or infusions to restore levels. IDA is linked to higher risks of disease progression and hospitalization, making proper management essential. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! Salt and Hydration: Time for some facts! Intestinal inflammation in IBD can affect nutrient absorption, leading to imbalances in sodium, chloride, and calcium levels, and increased potassium loss. Dehydration can also be an issue due to diarrhea, vomiting, or having a stoma. So, should you add salt to your water? Yes and no! For most people, a balanced diet should be enough to replenish electrolytes. However, if you’re experiencing significant fluid loss (e.g., from vomiting, persistent diarrhea, or after intense exercise), adding a pinch of salt to your water can help. Sodium draws water into cells, supporting hydration. Just remember, only a pinch! Too much salt can have negative health effects. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! IBD specialist nurses are a huge source of support to people with Crohn’s and Colitis. This is the woman who started it all: Sheila Phillips. She set up her clinic in Weymouth in 1993, and changed the face of IBD care forever. Sheila tells us her story and reflects on how IBD nursing has changed over the years. “I was working as a clinic nurse and we used to see quite a lot of patients with Crohn’s and Colitis. I got to know one of the young women on our books quite well, so when I saw her sitting outside the clinic one day, I went over for a chat. She had been diagnosed with Colitis and was looking a bit lost. I thought: ‘My goodness, she just needs to be able to talk to somebody’. So, that’s what gave me the incentive to start looking into a way of empowering patients with knowledge. With the support of my consultant, I set up my IBD nursing service. Soon, I was travelling all over the UK, with encouragement from the Royal College of Nursing, speaking at conferences about my work. Other nurses started coming down to Weymouth to have a look at what I was doing, and it kept growing from there. I can’t believe how much IBD nursing has grown since those days. Crohn’s & Colitis UK has an IBD nurse specialist programme now, with nurses who are able to prescribe, and it’s just incredible. One thing that hasn’t changed at all is that information is at the centre of it all. It’s still really important. If you’re going to be able to take responsibility for your own health, then you need information.” Read Sheila's story and learn more about he history of IBD nursing that has shaped national care, today, go to our link in bio, under 'Awareness Week' click Sheila' story #ibdreport #crohnsandcolitisawarenessweek #crohnsandcolitisawarenessweek2024 #crohnsawareness #ibd #crohnsandcolitis #crohns #crohnsdisease #colitis #crohnsandcolitisuk #ulcerativecolitis #inflammatoryboweldisease

Do you notice red marks in you after using a hot water bottle? Using a hot water bottle for IBD-related abdominal pain?  You might develop erythema abigne, a rash caused by chronic heat exposure. It appears as redness or a net-like pattern on the skin. While heat provides relief, if you rely on it often, it might signal an underlying issue like a flare-up. If you’re using heat frequently, it’s time to talk to your doctor about better ways to manage your IBD symptoms. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! Living with IBD impacts people’s lives far beyond the gut, Hakeem was at university when he realised how intwined mental health and chronic illnesses can be. Living with Crohn’s, he decided to change his path from music to mental health, applying for a postgraduate Mental Health Nursing course.   Hakeem said: "Finding community in chronic illness reminds us that while our journey is personal, we don't have to walk it alone. Researchers believe there’s a link between psoriasis and IBD, with people who have psoriasis being at a higher risk of developing IBD. Psoriasis is a chronic condition caused by immune system dysfunction, leading to inflammation throughout the body—most commonly affecting the skin. The most common type, plaque psoriasis, causes skin cells to multiply too quickly, forming raised, scaly patches. A 2018 study found that people with psoriasis are 2.5 times more likely to develop Crohn’s disease and 1.7 times more likely to develop ulcerative colitis compared to those without psoriasis. There’s also growing evidence that the gut and immune system are closely linked. A 2019 study suggested that gut inflammation, potentially caused by an imbalance of bacteria, could be a risk factor for both psoriasis and IBD. Interestingly, both conditions are often treated with similar medications, including biologics and steroids. Let me know your thoughts in the comments! I was diagnosed with Colitis back in 1992, just weeks out from going for my third Olympic Gold in Barcelona. I’d had what I thought was food poisoning a couple of years earlier in South Africa, and the intense stomach cramps I was getting made me think I’d eaten something dodgy again.  I was in the loo 10 times a day. Matt Pinsent, who I was rowing with, was doing really well and my scores should have been stronger than his, but they were really tailing off. My wife is a doctor, so she took me to see a specialist who mentioned Colitis but said: “There’s no way it can be that with what you’re managing to do.” But he booked me in for tests, and I remember we had to pull over onto the hard shoulder on the way home so I could be sick. The stomach pains I was getting were horrendous. When they said it was Colitis, I was shocked. I didn’t know what it was. I started on some treatment and, luckily, my performance began coming back.  But it was a really close call. I was so nervous when we got to Barcelona. I remember the hairs on the back of my neck standing up after we got through the first race. I thought: "OK, we're back to where we should be, we're going to be Olympic champions." And we were! When I won the gold medal I wasn't thinking much about my Colitis. But when I got home, the stomach cramps returned. I was bent double in agony with a horrible flare. When I look back at it now, I realise I was a very sick individual a few weeks before the Games and then, a matter of weeks after the Olympics, I was back to being really sick. Who knows was there that two month period in the middle when I was really healthy and good enough to become an Olympic champion for the third time? It must have been so hard for Matt to have a partner whose performance was so up and down. But that's camaraderie and team spirit for you. You're individuals, but you're nothing without the people around you. The treatment I’m on now works for me and I’ve mostly been in remission, plus I’m married to a doctor, so I’m in good hands. Not everyone’s that fortunate and I know that. Some people have a terrible time with these conditions and I count myself lucky in some respects. Normal Blood Tests, But You Don’t Feel Normal?  Time for some facts! It’s incredibly frustrating when your blood tests come back normal, but you still don’t feel right. I know this feeling all too well, especially when I went undiagnosed for a year with Crohn’s Disease! In medicine, there’s a saying: “”Treat the patient, not the results.”” While tests like bloodwork and scans are important, they don’t always tell the full story. Normal results don’t mean you’re in the clear—sometimes, they simply don’t catch the underlying issue. For those with IBD, symptoms can fluctuate, and tests may not always correlate perfectly with how you feel. Conditions like IBS, endometriosis, or fibromyalgia can mimic IBD symptoms like bloating, diarrhea, and constipation—making it even harder to get a diagnosis. And let’s not forget: false negatives are always a possibility. Tests might not be sensitive enough, the disease might not be active at the time, or human error could be at play. So, if your tests come back clean but you still feel sick, it doesn’t mean your symptoms aren’t valid. If you feel like your concerns aren’t being taken seriously, remember: you can seek a second opinion. Let me know your thoughts on this in the comments! Let me explain… Before I explain, do you think IBD is the same as IBS? Many of you may have heard the terms IBD and IBS being interchanged for one another as if they were the same thing. While it is true that both present with similar symptoms, can be triggered by similar things, they are however not the same. IBD is classified as an actual disease that causes intestinal destruction due to inflammation while IBS is defined as a syndrome, or a disorder of gut function brought about by the control of the gut-brain axis (GBA). Furthermore, the differences don’t stop there as you can see IBD when diagnostic imaging (x-ray, CT, MRI, and ultrasound scans) are used whereas you can’t see IBS on these scans and IBD is associated with an increased risk of developing colon cancer whereas IBS is not. Even though symptoms of IBS (bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and constipation) are like IBD, there are so many other features that separate the two. For example, IBD is associated with fatigue, weight loss, generally feeling unwell, loss of appetite as well as mouth ulcers whereas none of these are present in IBS. The most obvious difference between the two is that the ‘inflammation’ in IBS does not cause destructive damage to the intestines in addition to there is no bleeding after bowel movements in IBS unlike in IBD further differentiating the two. Crohn’s & Colitis awareness week 💜 Part 2 of my IBD story.  I went into a major flare up when I was 22 in 2019 at the time I was on holiday and I had lost an extreme amount of weight, everything I was eating I couldn’t hold down and my stomach pains were excruciating. I couldn’t get of bed and would be curled up in a ball hoping it would pass, it of course did not. Once i got home I was admitted into hospital and my meds changed, I was put onto prednisolone (steroids) aswell as being tube fed. I also had these lumps on my shin that felt bruised but wouldn’t go and this is called Erythema nodosum, this can happen when you have a flare up but I was told it is very rare. I was in for several weeks and sent home on steroids I still wasn’t right and a month later I was back in hospital in even worse pain still on steroids but the dosage was higher. Yet again I was in hospital for several weeks feeling worse than ever. My mental health was at an all time low and I thought these pains were never going to go away. The steroids now at this point kicked in and I was sent home for the final time that year (November 2019).  I then went through the last month and the following year through Covid on steroids at the highest dose and as you can see in pictures Moon face appeared. I was still not at a good weight and I also had started a new infusion Vedolizumab. I had this for a few months but it did not work for me so they carried on giving me steroids. My fatigue was at an all time low, my mood swings on the steroids were terrible and during Covid this wasn’t good (2020) Fast forward to January 2021, I developed a rectovaginal fistula and was admitted to have a seton placed for the fistula. I was sent home but the pain of it was unbearable and things got worse throughout January.   February my health declined and the pain was excruciating i couldn’t sit and would scream in pain. I was admitted and had been told I now had Sepsis and I needed a Stoma bag the following day to give everything a rest and time to heal. I was so scared but knew it was the only way but most importantly this was going to save my life.
